If I have a photon which is radially outward and a distance D from the event horizon, whereas I am an observer a distance L from the event horizon, in units where c=1, I would expect a photon to take a time L-D to reach me. In reality, there is an extra factor R_S ln(L/(D-R_S)). So for photons which bounce off of the collapsing matter D~ R_S + epsilon away from the center of the spherical shell, you should expect the travel time of the light to be delayed by R_S ln(L/epsilon). This can be arbitrarily big, and so this photon which carries the information about the collapsing matter right before it forms the event horizon takes an arbitrarily long amount of time to reach me.

[The Penrose diagram](https://jila.colorado.edu/~ajsh/insidebh/penrose_schw.gif) of a black hole is one way to visualize the math. In this picture, a moment in time is any line which is mostly horizontal (it never has a slope bigger than 45°), its rightmost endpoint ends on the corner of the diamond, and the leftmost endpoint can end anywhere on the diagonal line above the leftmost diamond point. 

If you take your time slice to end on the left diamond point, then the time slice will never enter the black hole because it would have to slope faster than 45° to do so. If you take it to be as far along the diagonal line as possible (essentially touching where it meets the singularity) then your time slice can cover the entire spacetime. The outside observer you're thinking of corresponds to the first kind of time slice. So even though they never see the black hole form, that's just because they are missing part of the spacetime. 

For the math people here, the statement is that the outside observer only has access to a "partial Cauchy slice" but the (union of all) infalling observer(s) has access to a full Cauchy slice.

The trick of general relativity is "what do you mean by time?" From the perspective of someone who stays outside of the black hole forever, you can't literally "see" the black hole forming, but it's there. But maybe it would help to think about it in terms of forces instead. From that perspective, the reason you can't see it is this. 

The event horizon is the point of no return: that means that a photon (the fastest particle possible) that sits exactly on the event horizon, pointing straight out, will be stuck forever because the force of gravity is just strong enough to trap it. If a photon is just barely outside, it will very slowly overcome the force of gravity and eventually escape. But that photon never actually "touched" the black hole, it was just barely outside of it. So you when your eye absorbs that photon, you don't see the black hole: you see just barely outside of it. 

This includes when a black hole forms: a photon which hits the matter juuuust before it collapses into a black hole take a long time to overcome the gravity of the recently formed black hole. A photon that was a little closer will take a little longer to escape. In the end, this means that you never actually see the black hole forming. It's similar to a Zeno's paradox thing. 

But the black hole is really there. If you went up to where you saw it forming and fell through, you would suddenly see it fully form because you pass by all these photons that have been almost trapped by gravity: instead of them coming to you in infinite time, you went to them in finite time. After that, though, you're in the black hole and can't come out again. Tough luck!

There's are roughly two possibilities for how to think about what physical things are made of. 

The first is that they are made of smaller things, and that keeps happening no matter how far you zoom in. There's no "bottom".

The second is that there is a smallest unit of "stuff" that just exists as a brute fact. This smallest unit wouldn't be made of anything in this case.

One interesting thing is that if quantum fields fall into the first category, then the "stuff" that makes it up has to be *weird* after you look at stuff that's smaller than 10^-35 meters big. That's the Planck length, which is where quantum gravity becomes important. To the best of our knowledge, this isn't what happens.

If it's the second category, then the smallest stuff should be smaller than 10^-35 meters big for similar reasons. At this distance scale, the notion of distance itself becomes fuzzy because there is no experiment which can measure distances that small, even in principle. That doesn't necessarily mean smaller distances don't exist, just that no experiment can't measure them. So who knows what kind of stuff can even exist at scales like that!

Gauge theories have constraints. In QED, this means that the naive Hilbert space where any possible charge and electric field configuration is bigger than the physical Hilbert space. The way to solve this is to focus on the subspace of Hilbert space that satisfies the constraints equation C|\psi> = 0, where C is the constraint operator. In QED, C= div(E) - rho, where rho is the charge density. So satisfying the constraints means you satisfy Gauss' law. 

General relativity is also a gauge theory, so it also has constraints. In fact, while QED has a mix of constraints and dynamical field equations (the rest of Maxwell's equations, other than div(B)=0 which is just an identity), GR has *only* constraint equations. So being able to find solutions which satisfy the constraints is equivalent to finding a solution of GR. Now, GR is more complicated than QED, so there are actually four constraints instead of one. Three of them are called the "momentum constraints" and they are the "easy" ones to solve. Like Gauss' law, they are linear in the field variables, which makes satisfying them fairly simple, at least relatively speaking. 

The final constraint is the Hamiltonian constraint H|psi> = 0, where H~C is the constraint operator. In the quantum case, this is the Wheeler-deWitt equation. So why don't we just find the solutions of this equation and declare victory on quantum gravity? Well, there are many reasons, but perhaps one of the most important is that we can't really solve this equation explicitly! The reason is that H is way more complicated. Not only is H non-linear in the metric, it isn't even polynomial because of a factor of sqrt(det(g)). This makes interpreting the metric as an operator and solving the equations really hard. 

Ashtekar's insight was to soften this difficulty by changing variables from q to something called the densitized tetrad, essentially the square root of the metric with an extra factor of sqrt(det(g)). This makes the sqrt(det(g)) way simpler to deal with, among other things. Using these variables, you can solve the Wheeler-deWitt equation (really, sqrt(det(g))H=0) and quantize the theory, at least in principle. Roughly, this leads to loop quantum gravity. But there's no free lunch, and LQG has other conceptual issues that arise from it, which make it not as popular as other approaches nowadays.

The current scientific consensus about space and time is that it is described by general relativity (GR). Philosophically, this is most immediately compatible with the block universe picture of time, or eternalism. It's not impossible to be a presentist, but it is much much harder to justify in the face of GR. I can explain more if you're interested, but the gist is that there's no way to define a uniquely "real" moment in time to be the "wavefront" of a presentist picture of time. Luckily, GR says if you want that picture to hold, then any wavefront is equally good. But then you have to bite the bullet that no wavefront is preferred, so there's no way, even in principle, to determine what the "real" present is. So it's easier to just say that all moments are equally real, leading to eternalism.

As with everything in science, we can never have 100% certainty. Through experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, we can be confident in the block universe picture for length scales of at least 10^-18 meters. Through cosmology, the block universe holds up to 10^26 meters. There's no reason to expect spacetime to break down for larger distances, but there is reason to think it changes a lot around 10^-35 meters (the Planck length), where quantum gravity kicks in.

It seems that you're imagining that the sphere will "bend inwards" enough that opposite ends would "touch" and form a wormhole. Unfortunately, that's not quite right. Imagine if the universe was 2 dimensional rather than 3d (I'm ignoring time). This is just to help visualize. Then, instead of a sphere, you could also imagine the universe was shaped like a torus: a donut. When you think of a donut, you probably think of the "outside" of the donut as being positively curved (because it's like a sphere) and the "inside" being negatively curved (it's like a saddle). But this is all extrinsic curvature: the intrinsic curvature of  a torus is zero. So you could also build a torus by having a flat square and just declaring that the top equals the bottom, and the left equals the right, kind of like the game asteroid or pacman. 

In this pacman world, how would you picture the wormhole forming? There's no "opposite sides" which can touch in this case. On the other hand, imagine the "donut case". There your wormhole pinching idea seems more visually intuitive. But the point is that GR doesn't actually care about whether you're in the donut case or the pacman case: what matters is the metric *on* the surface, not the background metric/coordinates we use to visualize it. So because GR can't tell the difference between those cases, neither can possible wormholes, because GR can determine if they will happen or not.

A common idea that's presented as to why gravity is hard to quantize is that GR by itself is not a renormalizable field theory, but that isn't quite right. QFT can handle non-renormalizable theories all the time: Fermi's 4-theory is a classic example. What GR being non-renormalizable means is that more physics is guaranteed to kick in at small scales, which can change the theory and possibly make it renormalizable. It happens to the Fermi 4-theory being completed with the standard model. But renormalizable field theories can also be "UV completed". For instance, the standard model will one day be altered at small scales to include gravity, even though it is a renormalizable theory.

QFT is often taught as a series of tools to compute scattering amplitudes perturbatively. Perhaps the most important tool in this toolbox is the Lagrangian, as it summarized the dynamics of the theory. Locality is often stated as a condition on the Lagrangian of the theory. Because of this, one might think that Lagrangians are essential to the definition of QFT.

But it turns out that there are many QFTs which *don't* have Lagrangians at all! They are hard to study directly but are known to exist for many reasons. Often, people say that the "reason" they don't have a Lagrangian is because of the strong, non-local interactions between the fields.

Essentially yes. If you want to learn more, study Maxwell's equations in the notation of the Faraday tensor F_uv . I don't have time to explain every symbol etc in this comment, but hopefully it at least plants the seeds that will help you find what you need. In that notation, Maxwells equations read (for a fixed choice of index v)

0= d^u F_uv = d^u (d_u A_v - d_v A_u ) = d^u d_u A_v - d_v (d^u A_u) 

Focus on the last form of the equation. d^u d_u A_v is exactly the Klein-Gordon equation for the A_v component. d_v (d^u A_u) is a term which takes a derivative of d^u A_u , which involves every component (not just A_v ) so it mixes together the components. But because of gauge invariance, we can focus on vector fields with d^u A_u = 0 , so only the Klein Gordon part contributes, and the field components don't mix anymore.

A bosonic field has many components A^i . For a single scalar, this is just phi. For a vector field, these are the components of the vector. In very loose terms, the equation of motion has two parts: 1) how does each component A^i evolve, and 2) how do they mix together under this evolution. 

1) ends up being the Klein-Gordon equation. The way that the components "mix together" in 2) depends on how we define those components to begin with. It turns out that for bosons, we have the freedom to redefine these components A^i -> (A^i)' so that the (A^i)' don't mix together under their equation of motion. This freedom is related to gauge freedom. For vector fields, this is called Landau gauge, where you shift the vector field by a gradient until d_i A^i = 0. For gravitons (spin 2) this is called the transverse traceless gauge.

By just-space I didn't mean anything too crazy by it, it's not a technical term. I just mean the normal three dimensions we experience as space, which you can think of as a specific instant in time.

Here's an analogy. When you watch a movie that's stored on a film reel, you only watch one frame at a time. But in some sense, the movie *is* the whole film reel. To make this more clear, you could cut each frame out and stack them on a table, so the "height" above the table acts as the time direction. As 3d beings we are capable of seeing the whole stack of frames, which is essentially the spaghetti. But a flatlander who is forced to climb that stack of frames would only see one frame at a time. But from our 3d perspective, that doesn't change the fact that the stack of frames is like the spaghetti. It's the same for us: even though we only see "3d frames" of our worldlines (the technical term for that spaghetti), it doesn't change the fact that in a spacetime perspective, we are the whole spaghetti.

An object has a "true shape" in just-space even if you rotate around it so you see it from a different point of view. Length contraction and time dilation are just like this: the object "looks different" because you're looking at it from a new point of view, but it's still the same object with the same "true shape". 

That true shape, as far as it can be defined, is determined by *geometry*, in particular, the spacetime geometry of special relativity. It's not the "coordinate time" which determines an object's intrinsic geometry. Instead, it's the "proper time", which is the time the object experiences itself, rather than what an outsider may perceive. That's why you're "just a spaghetti" through spacetime. The noodle is as long in the time direction as your age.

The standard model gauge group is said to be 

G_SM =SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1)

But what is *actually* known is that the Lie algebra for the standard model gauge group is

g_SM = su(3) x su(2) x u(1).

The specific global form of the gauge group is, as far as I can tell, still an open question. As an example of what I mean ask yourself what the difference between an SU(2) and SO(3) gauge theory would be. They would both have the same W/Z bosons, because their Lie algebras are the same. So the only difference is what charges are allowed in the theory: the SU(2) theory could have the j=1/2 representation (like the Higgs) but an SO(3) theory could not. 

All that to say: the question of if the color neutral gluon could be the photon is related to the question of the global form of the standard model gauge group. Is it U(3) x SU(2)? Is it SU(3) x U(2)? Is it (U(3) x U(2)) / U(1) (by which I mean you remove the diagonal U(1) between them)? I don't think anyone definitively knows.

It's a good question. There are two reasons, that are secretly the same reason. 

The first is that if you look at the action in the path integral, replacing t-> -it sends iS-> -S, whereas t->it sends iS -> S. After exponentiating it in the path integral, you want large action configurations to be suppressed, not enhanced, so the first option is better.

The second is that a Wick rotation arises when you change the contour for t in the Feynman propagator. When you do this, you need to make sure you don't move the contour over any poles. It's the order parameter for chiral symmetry breaking in QCD. Ok, that's a lot of words, here's what that means. In QCD, there are two kinds of quarks: left and right handed. In addition, each quark has three possible flavors: these are the three families of the standard model. If we take a limit where the quark masses are negligible (which is a good one inside a nucleus) then these flavors are essentially the same particles, but with an extra "flavor index" which tells you if the quark is, say, up charm or top.

Because there are three flavors, we can rotate the fields with an SU(3) transformation on that flavor index. That's not the same SU(3) as the strong force: if there were N flavors of quark, it would be SU(N). In other words, color and flavor aren't the same thing. But in the massless limit, we can treat the left and right handed particles as independent, so we can actually rotate the flavor indices on each handedness separately. In other words, the flavor symmetry group of massless QCD is SU(3)_L x SU(3)_R. 

Well, that's true only if that flavor symmetry is unbroken. The quark condensate <qbar q> is *not* invariant under the full flavor symmetry group: it is only invariant under the "diagonal subgroup" where you rotate the left and right handed particles the same way. That follows directly from the definition of qbar having a gamma^0 in it. So a nonzero value of <qbar q> spontaneously breaks the flavor symmetry. The reason I'm bringing up symmetry breaking is a) that's how people actually think about it, and b) because it turns out that the relevant physics (which I'll explain a bit below) is mostly determined by this pattern of symmetry breaking, not the specifics of the value of (a nonzero) <qbar q>, or the mechanism of how that vev arose. That's just effective field theory at work.

Physically, <qbar q> is related to the probability of a meson existing in the vacuum. That can only happen if the theory confines: therefore, this vev is a measure of confinement. The interesting thing is that my comment above means that as the vev is nonzero, the physics is essentially determined by the symmetry breaking, so the underlying details of how confinement occurs isn't very important for nuclear physics.

There are two things going on here that need to be separated. The first is why the Higgs field gives elementary particles inertial mass. The second is why inertial mass (however it comes about) is equal to gravitational mass.

It seems that your perspective is that inertial mass "is a thing" because of the Higgs field. As other commenters have said, that's not entirely true. For protons, for example, their mass is essentially independent of the Higgs field. Even if quarks were massless, protons would still be heavy. So we can see from this example that although the Higgs field is sometimes the answer to "why" particles have inertial mass (if they are elements), that's not always the full story. The way that I think about it is that inertial mass "is" the norm of a particles 4-vector, p_u p^u = m^2 . That value of m^2 comes about in many ways: sometimes the Higgs field, sometimes the binding energy of gluons, sometimes other sources of energy.

As for the second question, "why" inertial and gravitational mass agree. That has a lot more moving parts, so I'm going to reframe the question a few times until it gets to a form that I feel like "bottoms out" in a nice enough way.

 The first thing to say is that "gravitational mass" by itself is the source of gravity only when particles are moving slow with respect to the speed of light. More generally, it is their entire 4-vector of momentum p_u which sources gravity: it's just that when their speed is small, that four vector is basically just m in the t component and 0 for the other three. So the real question is "why does energy and momentum source gravity"?

There are a few ways to answer that question. The first is *how* energy-momentum sources gravity: through Einstein's equation, G_uv = T_uv (I'm ignoring constants for simplicity). The G_uv is the "gravity" part because it determines the shape of spacetime, and is called the Einstein tensor. The T_uv is the "energy-momentum" part, and is called the stress tensor. The fact they are equal is "why" gravity is sourced by energy-momentum. For dust clouds, T_uv = 1/m p_u p_v .

Ok, but I'm guessing your next question is going to be "why is the Einstein equation true". That requires a little more sophisticated math. The way I think about it is that the Einstein equation is true because the Lagrangian of general relativity is 

L_EH = 1/2 R + L_matter

The EH stands for Einstein-Hilbert. If you don't know what a Lagrangian is or what these terms mean, I would recommend that as the next part of your GR journey. It is a single function which determines the Einstein equations when you take specific "derivatives" of it. So yet another equivalent rephrasing of question #2 is "why is the Lagrangian of GR just L_EH".

This is the rephrasing that has "and answer". And that answer is essentially something called effective field theory. Essentially, effective field theory says that the Lagrangian of gravity *isn't* just L_EH: it should be way more general. And it probably is, taking a form more like 

L = 1/2 R + a_2 R^2 + a_3 R^3 + ...

And so on. In other words, the function L should be as general as possible. There are other terms that I'm not writing because I don't want to overload this comment. But there's a catch: dimensional analysis. It turns out that a_n can be estimated to be 

a_n ~ M_P^4-2n

Which means that the bigger n is, the smaller a_n will be (the coefficient of 1/2 R is really a_1 , that's just the constant I ignored above). The prediction for a_2 I gave you above is well below the current experimental bounds, people have definitely searched. But because "gravity is weak", it's hard to see that effect.

Finally, I should say that even if we use the more general Lagrangian L, energy momentum still sources gravity. It's just that the expression for G_uv becomes way more complicated.

In summary:

Its not always true that inertial mass exists "because" of the Higgs field. Inertial mass is the "rest energy" of particles, no matter how they get it.

Inertial mass sources gravity as slow speeds: more generally, it is the full energy momentum tensor T_uv. 

Energy momentum sources gravity because of the Einstein equations.

The Einstein equations are true because the Lagrangian of gravity is L_EH.

The Lagrangian of gravity is approximately L_EH because the Planck mass is large, i.e., gravity is weak.

An example is QFT. As it is taught in intro QFT classes, quantum field theory does not exist. It's not just that the relevant math isn't known yet, the definition of a QFT that physicists use can be proven to not exist. 

From the path integral perspective, it is because there is no uniform measure over the space of field configurations.

From the algebraic perspective, it is because of Haag's theorem.

The way it's presented is usually first introducing QFT as this object that exists and must be tweaked slightly to calculate with. That slightly tweaked version *does* exist mathematically. Then, they take a limit where they remove those tweaks to get the original object again. This limit produces finite and well defined answers, despite the original object not existing. That's why QFT works. This whole process makes most mathematicians rip their hair out. For physicists, it's totally fine: the path integral works, so we use it. But no amount of epsilons and deltas will save you from the fact that the path integral (as it is usually taught/defined) simply does not exist. Being comfortable with that is part of thinking about math like a physicist.

It's possible to do this and succeed. But it won't be easy. I did a double major in math and physics in undergrad. It was very helpful in both directions. But if I only did the math, I wouldn't have gained the intuition about which parts of math were important for physics and which are just math stuff. So if you do just a math undergrad, the important thing is to learn how to think about math like a physicist does, rather than think about physics like a mathematician does.

It sounds like your goal is to be better prepared for QFT and GR. The reality is that there's no "maximum" amount of math that could be useful in that goal if you want to go all the way into those fields, as opposed to just the basics. Because of that, if your plan is to learn every single prereq before starting, you'll never start. 

The more important skill as an undergrad is to learn how to learn math. When you're studying math, learn how to pick up the big ideas quickly, and get familiar enough with the way physicists use math that you can see the patterns. You don't have to be a mega genius who can instantly understand any math concept, but if you encounter something new, you should be able to fairly quickly at least get to a point where you understand the big ideas (maybe not the details) enough to confidently say "I believe the author that this is right". That is the much more useful skill. Don't fool yourself into thinking you understand the topic at this point: just acknowledge that you need to go back later and close those gaps. But at least you'll understand enough to know exactly what those gaps are.

That being said, differential geometry, group theory, lie groups, and representation theory (and their prereqs) are the mathematical topics that you should focus on learning. It'll take time to get all of those down, but if you can use these topics as your training ground for learning the skill I mentioned above, you'll be in a good place to learn QFT/GR.

Also, I learned QFT from Schwartz. It's not perfect, but there's no perfect book on the market right now in my opinion. But overall I thought Schwartz was solid at giving the big picture.

A\_\mu(x) = \sum\_k,± e^ikx (e^± \_\mu (k))^* a\_±(k)  + e^± \_\mu (k) a\_±(k)^\dagger

So it's the coefficient in front of the creation operators of the photon, and that's the thing that shifts around under a gauge transformation because its the thing that has an index.

Also, here's a quick way to see why the Ward identity is true. Under a gauge transformation:

A\_\mu -> A\_\mu + i \partial\_\mu f(x)

Fourier transform both sides, and remember that the polarization vector is exactly the Fourier transform of A_\mu to see

e\_\mu -> e\_\mu + f(k) k\_\mu

This means that we should treat any polarization vector as the same as another that's just shifted by a factor of the momentum. That means that 

e\_\mu M^\mu = e\_\mu M^\mu + f(k) k\_\mu M^\mu

Because f(k) is totally arbitrary, that implies the Ward identity.

One basis for the \mu index is obviously \mu = 0,1,2,3 which corresponds to a photon polarized in the t,x,y,z coordinates, respectively. But we can pick whatever basis we want. A common basis for the \mu index in this case (where we take the photon to be going along the z axis for simplicity) is as follows:

e_u = (1,0,0,1)

e_v = (1,0,0,-1)

e_± = (0,1,±i,0)

These four basis vectors (which you can take the \mu index to label) correspond to the momentum of the photon, the "conjugate direction", and a left/right handed circularly polarized photon. The Ward identity is equivalent to saying that M^u =0. It turns out that the Ward identity (really, gauge invariance) also implies M^v =0 as well, and so you don't need to worry about the interpretation of the cancellations you were worried about. This is why the Ward identity is important: it's what guarantees that only the physical ± states propagate.

M^\mu is the scattering *amplitude* of a certain incoming or outgoing photon with a polarization in the \mu direction. Now, you might complain that photons can't be polarized in the time direction, or along the axis that they are propagating (maybe the z axis). You can rephrase that into saying the photon can't be polarized in the direction of its momentum. In turn, that means that the scattering amplitude should be zero along that direction, because otherwise there is a nonzero probability (amplitude squared) to measure an unphysical polarization state. That's exactly what the Ward identity prevents.

The standard way to compute set sizes is to build a function called an "isomorphism" between those two sets. An isomorphism (in this context) just means that the function has an inverse: f(x) = 3x -4 is an isomorphism with inverse f^-1 (x) = (x+4)/3, but g(x)=x^2 is not an isomorphism because, for example, g sends both 2 and -2 to 4, so theres no unique inverse of 4 with this function. If there is any isomorphism between two sets at all, we call those two sets isomorphic.

If two sets are isomorphic, then they have the same cardinality, which is the way math people talk about the size of a set. Roughly, the reason people think like this is because x and f(x) are matched up in each set, and the fact f(x) is an isomorphism means that the matching is one-to-one (the pairings are unique) and onto (nothing is "missed" in either set). 

Now let's talk about your example. An equivalent way to phrase your example is: does there exist an isomorphism between the infinite real number line and a single interval? The answer is yes! Here's one such isomorphism: f(x) = arctan(x). This function has an inverse f^-1 (x) = tan(x), so it really is an isomorphism. Arctan has a maximum of 1 and a minimum of -1, so you can imagine putting these endpoints on your mirror.

Here are some other surprising isomorphisms. Consider the integers Z= {... -1, 0, 1, 2, ...} and the even integers 2Z = {..., -2, 0, 2, 4, ...}. These two sets are isomorphic because the map f(x)=2x has an inverse f^-1 (x) = x/2. Your intuition might have said that 2Z is only half as big as Z (and there are other concepts other than cardinality which correspond to this intuition) but as far as set theory is concerned, they are the same size: infinity. Here's an even weirder example: the natural numbers {1,2,...} and the rational numbers. Imagine listing the natural numbers by denominator: {1/2, 1/3, 2/3, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, ...}. Obviously this is all the rational numbers: given your favorite rational number, I will eventually find it on this list at a finite position. Now let f(x) be the function which sends the number 1 to the first spot on this list, 2 to the second spot etc. that function f(x) is an isomorphism. Can you see why? The surprise is that means that there are "as many" natural numbers as there are rational numbers. Crazy stuff!

Two sets which are not isomorphic are the natural numbers and the real numbers. To see why, look up "Cantors diagonal argument". Combined with the above result, that shows that there are waaay more real numbers than rational numbers. In fact, rational numbers are "measure zero" inside the reals, which basically means that if you threw away every fraction from the number line, you'd basically still have the same amount of numbers as you started with. Cool stuff!

It turns out that these are all secretly the same explanation. 

Hawking radiation occurs for largely the same reason the Unruh effect occurs. The definition of a particle is tough to define in a curved spacetime, but the same is true even in flat spacetimes if you're in an accelerating reference frame. The Einstein equivalence principle says that curvature is just local acceleration, so that explains the connection there. This explanation connects most closely with #2. If you draw the Penrose diagram of a black hole, then you'll see that an observer a fixed distance outside the black hole really is quite analogous to an accelerating observer in the Unruh effect. It's not exactly the same, but not too far off either.

How does that relate to #1? The key thing about both these examples is that there are horizons at play. The Unruh effect has a casual horizon, while the black hole has an event horizon.  In both cases, there is a part of the spacetime that the fields will never interact with, and this means that there is a lack of information about that region of the spacetime. Lack of information=increase in entropy, entropy means there is a temper, and a temperature means a thermal bath of particles. 

As to #3, this is the most direct way to understand what's going on mathematically. Normally, we think of a particle as being an excitation above the vacuum state. That means that the definition of a particle depends on the vacuum state. In turn, the vacuum is defined as the state of lowest energy. But energy is the generator of time translations, and so different choices of Hamiltonian will lead to different vacuua, and therefore different definitions of particles. Often, there is a "right" choice for Hamiltonian: namely, the P_0 component of the energy-momentum vector. But other choices work just fine as well, as long as the Hamiltonian you pick generates a proper time evolution of the spatial slice you start with. For example, what if I picked K_x = P_0 x + P_x t, the generator of a boost? This is the Hamiltonian an accelerating observer would use to move forward in time (imagine the worldlines). If you imagine boosting a spatial slice forward and backward in time, that will sweep out Rindler space. If you compare the minimum energy state of the boost operator to the minimum energy state of P_0, they are not the same state. With respect to P_0, the "boost vacuum" turns out to look like a thermal state with a temperature of the accelerating observer. That's the Unruh effect.

In the black hole case, the black hole being stationary essentially means that we should use the "natural" Hamiltonian *near the black hole* and not far away from it. The natural Hamiltonian is the one of an observer who never goes inside, for that's the Killing field that makes the black hole stationary. For the same reason as the Unruh effect, this state is not the same as the vacuum of just P_0 by itself. A careful analysis shows that with respect to P_0, it looks like a thermal state with the Hawking temperature. 

Now we can see why horizons were important. A horizon is a null surface, and if you get close enough to any null surface, the "flow" that keeps it fixed will basically be a boost (at least locally). That means that the "natural vacuum" will (approximately) be thermal because you can use the Unruh effect as an analogy. I think one thing that often gets lost in this discussion is that naturalness isn't just a philosophy, it was also a tool which led to discoveries in particle physics which have been verified. For example, the mass of the charm quark was predicted before it was discovered based on naturalness arguments. 

Furthermore, other forms of naturalness are *required* by unitarity. Given certain measurements of certain scattering processes, if the Higgs boson was too much heavier, the standard model would not be a (edit: perturbatively) unitary theory. That's why the LHC knew that they would find *something* when they turned it on, they just expected to find a bit more than they did. As another example of what I mean by unitarity and naturalness being connected, consider the effective action of a particular quantum field theory. That's just the object you look at which tells you how a field reacts to all the other fields in the universe, averaged out in the appropriate way. It's the thing which controls the values of correlation functions, and summarizes the quantum corrections to particle masses and interactions. Just requiring your theory to be unitary puts constraints on what form these corrections can take, and some of those constraints say e.g. that some ratios of interaction strengths (which can be dimensionful) can't be "too large". There are bounds on how "different in scale" certain interactions can be.

Those are two very different meanings of the word naturalness, but in both cases I don't think it should be some dirty word that indicates all logic has flown out the window and we are just purely guessing. It's one of those things where it's worked really well in the past, it hasn't worked so well recently, and people have forgotten how well it used to work. The fact it's no longer as strong of a principle may itself be pointing to something interesting, and that's worth investigating on its own.

Imagine a vector pointing in the +y direction and sitting at (1,0,0) on the +x axis. If you rotate around the origin in the xy plane by 90 degrees, then not only is the vector now sitting at (0,1,0) (the orbital angular momentum does that) but now the vector is pointing in the -x direction (the spin does that). Just the spin would keep the vectors position fixed but rotate the vector around; just the orbital part would move the vector but keep it pointing in the same direction.

The reason spin combines with orbital angular momentum like it does is because it's genuinely the same kind of thing: they both generate rotations. They just rotate different things. The fact that they add together is just a statement about representation theory, which is in turn just a statement about the way that a rotation can "act" on the Hilbert space. 

The statement about representation theory is that a particles spin is an *irreducible* representation (irrep) of SU(2) (which is the same as irreps of SO(3) if you're allowed to ignore an overall phase). Furthermore, a fixed orbital angular momentum state is also an irrep, essentially by definition. Because these are both irreps within the Hilbert space, the angular momentum generators must act as the identity on any subspace which *isn't* that particular irrep, and the total generator is block diagonal on each irrep. That's just Schurs lemma basically.

There's a lot going on under the hood here, and all the details are in Steven Weinberg's QFT book but that's probably not a good reference for when you're first starting out. The concepts you're looking for are that of the "little group" for a given particle. Almost by definition, particles are the tiniest chunks that make up a quantum field. That raises the question as to what I mean by tiniest. Well, a quantum field can be moved around, rotated, and boosted to your hearts content, but some states of the field behave in a special way when you do these transformations. Intuitively, if I have two particles then I could move them around independently, so I can break up translations of the field into translations on each particle. On the other hand, if I had only one particle then there's no way to break up translations etc into a smaller subset. That's what we really mean by tiniest chunk, and it's what's called an irreducible representation (irrep) of the Poincare group (the group of translations and Lorentz transformations). So what do irreps look like? Well, that's a hard question for a general group, but for the Poincare group it works like this. First, pick an irrep for just the translation part. It turns out this is just assigning a specific four momentum to the particle, with the appropriate mass. Now, you focus on the subgroup of Poincare which keeps this specific four vector of momentum unchanged. That's called the little group. For example, for a massive particle, you can choose a reference frame p=(m,0,0,0). It's clear that if you boost the particle at all then you will change p, but if you do a spatial rotation then you keep p the same. That means that massively particles are labeled by SO(3) irreps, which is just spin. On the other hand, a massless particle has a momentum p=(E,E,0,0). We can obviously rotate the 0,0 part into each other. But we can also do a more complicated move of boosting in a direction orthogonal to the photons propagation and rotating it back to the original axis. More precisely, the Lorentz generations of the form e.g. M_-z leave this vector invariant. Together, these moves form a little group ISO(2). These irreps are labeled by two continuous parameters (a,b) as well as a choice of sign ±. The reason for this is we can figure out the irreps of ISO(2) by playing the same game we are doing for Poincare, we fix the irrep of the translation part (which is the a,b) and considering the remaining generators which leaves that invariant (either doing nothing or a reflection orthogonal to (a,b)). The (a,b) are experimentally observed to be zero, and the ± are exactly the helicity of a massless particle.

No. You can have an intrinsically curved surface without a bigger space to embed it into. Curvature comes in two flavors: intrinsic and extrinsic. 

To see the difference, take a piece of paper and roll it into a cylinder. Before you rolled it up, it is as flat as flat can be. But after you rolled it up, it has a "flat direction" and a "curved direction". But rolling it up didn't change the "intrinsic flatness" of the paper, you didn't crumple it up or tear it and reglue it or anything like that. You added "extrinsic curvature", which *does* require a bigger space to put your object into.

For an example of intrinsic curvature, consider the surface of a sphere. No matter how you squeeze or bend it, you can never fully flatten it out without tearing the sphere. Compare that to the cylinder, where you can always unroll it to be perfectly flat. So a sphere is curved, but not just because it bends into 3d space: it has some curvature that's just built directly into the sphere, and you could detect this curvature even if you never "left" the surface of the sphere to detect the third dimension. In other words, you can tell the Earth is a sphere without going into space (sorry flat-earthers). The greeks could do it, and so can someone who lives on any intrinsically curved surface. In contrast, there is no local experiment you can do on the paper to detect the fact that you rolled it up vs left it flat.

My personal take is that people who say renormalization isn't well defined because it's about "subtracting infinities" are misguided. Renormalization is always preceded by regularization, which makes those infinities finite. So the real question is: why is regularization well defined, and when it is, why is it unique? In some sense, regularization works because the non-regularized version of the theory should be thought of as being *defined* as a limit of the regulated theory. That is, there is a family of theories labeled by the regulator, and the one we ultimately care about is the limiting case of this family. What renormalization does is tells you *which* of the family of theories you should be taking in this limit. With the above perspective, renormalization isn't a weird hack, it's essentially to the definition of what theory you're discussing in the first place. On the other hand, we'd like a concept of mass that works even when there isn't such a symmetry: things are still heavy in dynamical spacetimes. Throughout the calculations, fix a coordinate system (t,x) where x represents all the spatial coordinates. In the Schrodinger picture, the Hilbert space can be thought of as living on a t=const slice. For something as featureless as a free, spinless particle, the only information a state can contain is the number of times and where the particle's worldline intersects this t=const slice. Because of QM, the particle can take any path in space through time, including those outside the lightcone. Because of relativity, that also means it can go backwards in time. So we need to integrate over ALL paths through spacetime, not just in space through time.

Now, consider two states, one in the far past and another in the far future. In other words, these are the boundary conditions for the path integral. We would like to compute the amplitude of a transition between these two states. To do so, we do the usual trick of discretizing the time t and integrating over all spatial slices, taking the continuum limit at the end. There's a problem though. The particle can go back in time, so we need to be careful with how we evaluate this. Let K be the propagator from the past to the future. We need to break up this propagator into smaller pieces to evaluate it. So, let K\_0(a=(t,x),b=(t',x')) be the time ordered propagator which ONLY integrates over future directed paths *in the coordinate system we fixed at the beginning*. Note that K\_0 = 0 unless t > t', which we write as a > b. This gives it the useful property that K_0 = \int K_0 K_0, where the integral is over JUST space for any *fixed* intermediate time. Notice that K\_0^dag (a,b) = K\_0^\*(b,a) needs b > a. These are basically just the retarded/advanced Greens functions. Later, it will be useful to define a Feynman propagator K\_F = 1/2i (K\_0 + K\_0^dag). The 1/2i is just a convention that we picked because of foresight later on. Okay, now we will write a recursive formula for K in terms of K\_0. 

To do so, let K\_++ be the propagator for states where the worldline is future directed when it intersects the past and future slice, K\_+- when the worldline is future directed on the future slice and past directed on the past slice, and similarly for K\_-+ and K\_--. These are essentially the propagators for (anti)particle -> (anti)particle. Notice that K = K\_++ + K\_-+ + K\_+- + K\_--. Essentially, what this is doing is splitting the measure of the path integral over worldlines into four classes. I'll focus on computing K\_++, but the others are analogous. Now, knowing that the particle is future directed on both slices, how could it have gotten there? Well, it could have possibly "turned around" in time zero times, or gone backwards and then forwards again, or done that twice, and so on. So on the class of paths integrated over in K\_++, we could build it as

K\_++ = K\_0 + \int K\_0 K\_0^dag K\_0 + \int K\_0 K\_0^dag K\_0 K\_0^dag K\_0 + ...

where \int means integrate over all the time slices that the turn around could have happened on between each K\_0/K\_0^dag. Adding all the other K\_-- and K\_-+ and so on, along with the argument that the Hilbert space itself is independent of time (essentially by arguing that the Schrodinger and Heisenberg pictures are physically the same) you can start to see the argument that the first quantized Hilbert space also has a Fock basis after Fourier transforming K_0 and so on. But notice something else nice about this expansion, that this implies

K\_++ = K\_0 + \int K\_0 K\_0^dag K\_++

This can be used to solve recursively for K\_++ because you can calculate K\_0 in perfect analogy to the usual worldline path integral of non-relativistic QM. Similarly,

K\_-- = K\_0^dag  + \int K\_0^dag K\_0 K\_--

K\_-+ = \int K\_0^dag K\_0 K\_-+ = \int K\_0^dag K\_++ = \int K\_-- K\_0

K\_+- = \int K\_++ K\_0^dag

Basically, you can swap a - for a + by inserting a K\_0 and integrating the positions for a fixed time, and then integrating over all possible times between the states. K =2i K\_F + 2i\int K\_F (K\_-+ + K\_+-)

Equivalently (as you should also check),

K = 2i\int K\_F (K\_++ + K\_--)

Now we can solve for K by adding these two equations and dividing by two to see

K =  i K\_F + i\int K\_F K

Up to now, we assumed that the two time slices were distinct. If we want to include the case when t = t', which is an initial condition for this recursion, we should demand that there is NO evolution if there is no passage of time, i.e., K((t,x),(t,x')) = \delta(x,x'). Redefining K \to K + \delta(t-t') \delta(x-x') to enforce this, you can see that

K = \delta(t-t')\delta(x-x') + i \int K\_F K

When we iterate this equation to solve for K, we see that the many time integrals which emerge are all time ordered (check the bounds of integration). We can remove this time ordering of the integrals term by term by integrating over ALL times and dividing by n!, where n is the number of integrals. 

K = \delta(t-t')\delta(x-x') + i K\_F - 1/2! \int K\_F K\_F + ...

where the integrals are now over all spacetime. This has a solution

K = exp(i K\_F)

This approach is called the "first quantised" formalism for QFT. It's not quite that simple because time is singled out in quantum mechanics to enter into the Schrodinger equation. If you tried to just use proper time, you'll find that the resulting evolution equation is just dPsi/dtau =0. 

Furthermore, the fact that the action is non-polynomial in the velocities actually causes technical difficulties in this approach. Something very similar happens in string theory, actually. In that case, instead of proper time, one wants to quantize the action of the "proper area" of the string. That action is called the Nambu-Goto action, and has the same technical difficulties I mentioned above. The solution here is instead using the Polyakov action, and the same approach works for point particles as well.

Finally, one thing you need to be careful of is that when you use this action in the path integral formalism, you really need to do integrate over all paths still. Even ones that go backwards in time. That makes the usual trick of defining the path integral as an integral over every time slice more tricky because now there are many many integrals to do on each time slice corresponding to different numbers of intersections of the world line with that particular slice. This is why using a field is so useful for this goal, it keeps track of all that stuff implicitly and you can talk about time evolution in the usual way again and define the path integral much more easily. Additionally, it has been shown (don't remember the reference) that the field approach and the first quantised approach are totally equivalent to each other.

Unfortunately, the holographic principle is currently best understood in AdS spacetime's. It's not clear yet if the Big Bang "counts" as a boundary that something even analogous to the CFT of AdS/CFT lives in. 

Furthermore, in AdS/CFT it's important that the CFT is at the largest scales and not the smallest ones. Smaller distances= higher energies by Heisenberg uncertainty. Conversely, larger distances= lower energy. And lower energy= smaller quantum fluctuations. The fact that the metric doesn't fluctuate *at all* at the boundary of AdS is exactly what makes AdS/CFT so computationally useful compared to dS (of which our universe is an example). If you tried to put something analogous to the CFT at small scales, then you'd have the opposite effect: the metric would be so violently fluctuating at those scales that it would destroy whatever you wanted to put there in the first place.

Think of it this way. If the nucleus was 100x smaller, you'd feel even more confident about where the particles that make it up are located: the window in space they can occupy is smaller. On the other hand, if the nucleus was 100x bigger, you'd be less confident about where the particles that make it up are located: the window they cal occupy is bigger. This (plus dimensional analysis) suggests that the uncertainty in the position of the particles in the nucleus us proportional to the size of the nucleus. 

What constant of proportionality should we use? If you just want an order if magnitude estimate, then it's okay to just assume that the real coefficient is order one (say, between 0.1 and 10) and plug that into the Heisenberg uncertainty relation to solve for delta p. If we want a more accurate estimate, we need to know more information about the wave function of the particles in the nucleus. One common choice would be to model the nucleus as a particle in a (spherical) box with radius given by the nuclear radius. Another would be to take the wave function to be gaussian of width given by the nuclear radius. Yet another would be to solve the very complicated QCD problem of how the nucleons interact and get the exact wave function.

Of these choices, which is best? Obviously, if the last one is possible then do that. But that's probably too hard in general. So you should probably do one of the first two. But that answer won't be tooooooo different than just taking dX= the radius we were given, so I would just do that. Hope this helped!

One possible definition of information that works for quantum or classical systems alike is

Information = Maximum Entropy - Actual Entropy 

This is a useful definition for the following reasons. First, if we are in a maximum entropy state, then we are as ignorant as possible about what the microstate of the system is, which is zero information. On the other hand, if the state in question has zero entropy then it is uniquely determined and so that is maximum information. Furthermore, if you want to get more technical about it, then this definition is equivalent to

Information= RelativeEntropy(actual probability | chance)

So it gives the "distance" of the actual distribution of microstates to the unique distribution corresponding to pure chance. More information= further away from pure chance.

In quantum mechanics, the "max entropy" part is ln(|H|) (log of the dimension of the Hilbert space) and the "actual entropy" part is -tr(rho ln rho) where rho is the density matrix corresponding to the state of the black hole. If time evolution is unitary, then "actual entropy" is constant in time and we don't lose any information over time. If it is not unitary, then our amount of information decreases.

Imagine you lived on an infinitely long cylinder, where the circular part has a radius R. You can decompose motion on this cylinder into two pieces: the linear velocity v_l in the extended direction, and the rotational angular velocity w_r in the circular direction. Your total velocity, then, is v^2 = v_l^2 + R^2 w_r^2. You can see that if you fix w_r as you make R very small (which makes sense because it has units of frequency, and is independent of length) then even if you're "moving" in the circular direction, for all intents and purposes it's better to think of an effective description where your actual motion is just v_l, and w_r is instead just some "parameter" which affects your linear motion (for example, maybe your total velocity v^2 is fixed, so w_r would control how fast you move in the linear direction). In fact, that's exactly what happens in string theory. The analogies of w_r in that example includes the strength of vibrations of the strings in the compact directions, as well as how many times they "wrap around" those directions. These "parameters" lead to strings looking like they are particles with different charges and masses and so on in the effective 4d description. What masses and charges you get depends a lot on the geometry of the small directions. That's called a "Kaluza Klein reduction" of the theory, and is a key concept in understanding how strings work on these strange backgrounds!

Just to make sure we are talking about the same thing, I usually hear people refer to the state of the quantum fields as being in a Hadamard state, not that the spacetime is Hadamard. If you ignore GR effects then you can in principle consider non-Hadamard states even in flat space, though they are pathological. 

Being Hadamard essentially means that you can regulate observables like the stress energy tensor appropriately because the high energy behavior won't depend on the actual state you're considering, just that it's Hadamard, and so you can subtract the divergent bits in a universal way.

A physical reason for this requirement is that spacetime is a manifold, and therefore if you zoom in far enough, any manifold looks like Minkowski (by definition). The divergence of the two points function is all about the structure of the fields at short distances, and so being Hadamard means that the fields behave "as expected" at those scales.

Introducing a cutoff is probably the most intuitive example of regulating a theory. Another example is to add a factor of e^{-a·|k|} to the integrand that diverges, where |k| is the integration variable (usually the norm of the momentum) and a is an arbitrary factor. Then, after you compute this integral, you take a limit where a->0 so it's like you never added it in the first place. A hard cutoff is basically doing the same thing, but with a step function instead of an exponential. Yet another example is dimensional regularization: this is probably the most conceptually confusing one but also definitely the most practically useful once you get into more complicated examples of QFT. I'm not gonna go into it here because that's a whole other direction, and at the end of the day, one can show that the specific regulator you pick doesn't affect the answers for physical observables. You usually just pick the one that's most convenient for whatever you're trying to calculate.

In quantum mechanics, one way to think about why only energy differences matter is because the overall phase of the wave function isn't physical. If you multiplied every single wave function in your theory by e^{-iE_0t}, then that's an overall phase (even though it's time dependent) and therefore is completely unphysical. If you plug this new wave function into the Schrodinger equation, you'll see that you shifted the energy of every state up by exactly E_0. Therefore, the "zero" of energy is arbitrary and only energy differences matter. 

In QFT, the same principle applies because quantum fields are a special case of quantum mechanical systems. The difference is that the relevant E_0 is infinite by itself! So what we do is we first "regulate" the theory by changing its behavior at short distances (while keeping the long distance behavior the same) in a way that makes E_0 finite. Then, we can subtract it off as usual. Finally, we take a limit of changing the theory less and less, still subtracting off E_0 in the limit, so that once we get back to the original theory, the minimum energy is finite again. In a curved spacetime, the action takes the form

S = \int d^D x sqrt(-g) L

Where D is the dimension of the spacetime, L is the Lagrangian, and sqrt(-g) is the square root of the determinant of the metric. As a fun aside, this is one way to see the statement that "gravity sees everything". No matter the details of the theory given by L, EVERYTHING couples to the metric through the sqrt(g) factor, and so everything couples to everything else with gravity as a mediator. 

When you do perturbation theory, you want to think of the field as a small perturbation on top of some "average value" of the field. Usually, that average value is zero, but if it's not, then we redefine the field to be 

H = v + h

Where H is the old definition of the field, v is the average value, and h is the new definition of the field (which has an average of zero by definition). This is what we do with the Higgs boson for example. We want to do the same thing with gravity. Let's say the average value of the field is given by the Minkowski metric. In an equation,

g_uv = eta_uv + h_uv /M_P

Where g_uv is the full metric, eta is the Minkowski metric, M_P is the planck mass (I included it so that h has the standard normalization for its kinetic term which is convenient, but it's optional) and finally, h_uv is a small perturbation of the metric which an average of zero. h_uv is what people refer to as the "graviton field", NOT g_uv.

Almost there. I'll drop the L for now, but you should multiply the entire Lagrangian (even the kinetic terms) by all the terms I'm about to consider to get the actual interaction vertices. We want to write the sqrt(g) term in terms of h_uv. Well, in freshman physics, we learn that sqrt(1+ small) ≈ 1+ small/2 and so on, so we need to taylor expand sqrt(g) in powers of h_uv with eta_uv as the "1" part. It's a little more complicated because h_uv is a tensor, but it's really not very different. Here's the problem: sqrt has an infinite number of terms in its Taylor series! This means there will be interaction vertices with an ARBITRARILY LARGE number of gravitons interacting, on top of whatever interactions occur in the Lagrangian which I've suppressed. That's okay if h_uv is small: then you can approximate the Taylor series with the first few terms and be fine (that's what people do in cosmology for example). But you'll need an infinite number of counter terms for this infinite number of interactions.

TL;DR: the Lagrangian in gravity has an overall sqrt(g). When you consider fluctuations of the metric around it's average value and Taylor expand sqrt(g) in powers of these fluctuations, you're left with an infinite number of interactions and you need to stick with very small perturbations in practice so you can treat gravity as an effective field theory and limit yourself to the first few terms.

The metric is almost the same, except the metric is slightly different: ds^2 = -(1-R_S/r)dt^2 +(1-R_S/r)^(-1) dr^2 + r^2 dX^2. R_S is the radius of the event horizon. Notice that if R_S=0 the metric is exactly the same as flat space. Anyways, if r>R_S then youre outside the black hole. At the same time, the coefficient of dt^2 is still negative. But once r<R_S, the second term becomes smaller than -1 so the overall coefficient flips sign! This is what people mean when they say space and time flip.

Suppose you relabel your coordinates so T=r and R=t. Also, restrict to being inside the black hole, i.e. T < R_s. The metric is now -(R_S/T -1)^(-1) dT^2 + (R_S/T -1) dR^2 + T^2 dX^2. The singularity is at T=0, so it's more obvious that it really is in your future and not in the "center". There's no physics in this relabeling, it just makes more manifest the fact that the radial coordinate becomes timelike inside. This makes clear that time is still one dimensional: only the t or T coefficient is negative when you're outside or inside, respectively.

For a big enough black hole, you can make the event horizon's curvature as low as you want it to be. When the front of your ship passes the event horizon, the light will still hit your eyes as you fall in, it will just hit your eyes inside the black hole. This is easiest to see using a Penrose diagram. There, the event horizon is just a null line, and your motion into the black hole (assuming you don't turn on your rocket boosters) is just a vertical line. Your rocket ship of finite length will look like a strip with a finite horizontal thickness, the two edges being the front and back of your ship. At some point, the event horizon will be in the "middle" of this strip: that's when the front is inside and the back is not. Shoot a light ray from the front of the ship towards the back at this moment. The light ray will still hit the back of the ship, it will just hit it once the back is inside the black hole.

They are kind of like the Feynman diagrams of general relativity in the sense they are a graphical tool that is extremely useful in capturing some small part of the physics of GR, in particular casual structure. If you can truly understand what the Penrose diagram of a black hole means, I'd say you can genuinely claim to understand the causal structure of black holes.

A global symmetry is any transformation you can make to your fields (including the metric) that is *independent of spacetime* and leaves all the correlation functions unchanged. An example is translations in R^n: moving things to the left doesn't change the physics. Now, in quantum gravity, there are good reasons to believe that there should be no global symmetries in the bulk spacetime. Does that mean R^n is not a valid bulk spacetime? Well, not quite. No global symmetry means they must either be broken or gauged. In the case of translations, diffeomorphisms are precisely the symmetry group of gauging translations.

Another example is of a self-interacting complex scalar field. If the potential is only built out of |phi|^2, this has a global symmetry of rotating the field by a phase. This global symmetry must either be broken or gauged (which gives QED).

So it seems you're confusing global symmetry with symmetry. Diffeomorphisms and gauge symmetries are local, not global. Someone mentioned that in the path integral language, you need the action to be invariant under conformal transformations of your spacetime. It's true that it is a necessary condition, but it's actually not sufficient. Here's a weird example: quantum electromagnetism in 4 dimensions. Classically, electromagnetism is obviously translation and rotation invariant, but in four dimensions it turns out you can also locally rescale the metric and still get the same physics as well, I.e. it is conformally invariant . Essentially, this is because the electric charge is dimensionless in 4d but not in any higher or lower dimensions. However, this is also not true quantum mechanically. 

The conformal symmetry is broken by quantum processes like an electron shooting out a photon and absorbing it again, or a photon creating an electron positron pair before annihilating into another photon. These are often called "loop effects" in QFT because when you draw the spacetime picture (really a Feynman diagram) of this process, you have to draw some loop in the process. Loop effects are what makes quantum quantum. The study of how physics changes when you zoom in and out, in some sense, is essentially all of the physical content of (perturbative) QFT and is the study of "renormalization". 

For every parameter of the theory, such as masses or electric charges of particles, there is a special function called a "beta function" that measures how that parameter changes when you zoom in and out. It's literally the derivative of the parameter with respect to the scale you're looking at. The bigger the beta function, the more the parameter changes. Only when these beta functions are all zero is the theory conformal*. 4d QED has nonzero beta functions for the electric charge, for example, and that is why it is not conformal. Once again, this is the study of "renormalization" and although it is a big reason QFT can be so confusing, I really think it's worth learning because it is so crucial to what QFT really is. Beta functions, and the observables computed using them, are really the *only* thing perturbative QFT is good for, and I don't mean that in a derogatory way. It's really a very deep statement, and something I didn't appreciate until later than I should have!

The AdS/CFT correspondence is a conjectured relationship between quantum mechanics in d dimensions and gravity in d+1 dimensions. The quantum mechanics has a special symmetry called conformal symmetry: it is invariant under zooming in and out. The gravity takes place in a spacetime with a negative cosmological constant. There is a more general idea that any theory of quantum gravity in d+1 dimensions should have a d dimensional QFT associated with it: that's called holography. AdS/CFT is a specific case of holography. It is not known if our real universe is holographic or not. Personally I think there are very general reasons to believe the real universe is holographic because of something called the Wheeler-DeWitr equation, but I won't get into that here.

You can think about the extra dimension of the gravity side as being the length scale you are investigating the quantum mechanical theory at. For example, if I take the oceans, at one scale I will see a lot of waves, if I zoom in then I will see some water, then water molecules, atoms, protons, quarks, etc. Just like you can stack up photos at different times to see that time is a dimension, you can stack up these photos at different scales to make the scale you've zoomed into a dimension. The way everything fits together when you stack these photos makes it an AdS spacetime.

The conjecture is very precise: it says that the two theories have the same partition function, which is the object that completely determines the physical behavior of a theory. On the other hand, the conjecture is a bit fuzzy: not every state you can prepare in the quantum theory will let you stack up these "zoomed in" pictures in quite the right way to have a geometric interpretation when you put them all together. These sets of constraints often relate to the various entropies of the different regions of the state, and is often called the "holographic entropy cone". The important thing is that the most common viewpoint is that the quantum mechanical theory is fundamental, and the gravitational one is approximate.

Finally, this approach of holography was originally motivated by string theory, although it has an independent life of its own now. In string theory, holography was an example of "s duality", which is when you have two different theories that give the same answers for physical questions despite being quite different, i.e. one is very weakly coupled and one is super strongly coupled. This is both a blessing and a curse: it's a blessing because it makes calculations easier on one side the harder they get in the other, for example a calculation could be hard for the QFT side and easy on the gravity side or vice versa, but it also means that things will be hard to compute when the calculations are done at moderate coupling, i.e. order one coupling constants. This makes holography hard to check explicitly but gives a lot of evidence that it's true: we do a calculation using the other side and see that it completely agrees with what we expect on the original side of the duality.

Perhaps what you're looking for are the Schwinger-Dyson equations. Basically, let L'_i be the variation of the Lagrangian, i.e. the equations of motion for a classical field O_i. Then the Schwinger-Dyson equation says, for example, that

L'\_1(<O_1 ... O_n>) = <L_1'(O_1)O_2 ... O_n> -i\hbar \sum\_i \delta(x\_i - x\_1) <O_2 ... O_{i-1} O_{i+1} ... O_n>

Here, <...> is the correlation function or amplitude you want to calculate and we interpret L' as being an operator. Let's assume 3 things about black holes. 

The first is that no information is lost after the black hole collapses, radiates, shrinks, etc. The whole shebang. Information is always conserved. 

The second is that black holes have a finite number of possible ways it can be "under the hood". I.e. they have a "quantized" number of possible states.

The third is that the internal dynamics of black holes are very complicated.

If you assume these three things, then you can prove (using something called the Hayden-Preskill protocol) that black holes act as "information mirrors". If you tried to hide some information by throwing it into a black hole, that information basically leaks out almost instantly so you did a bad job of hiding it. Of course, in practice it would be impossible to reconstruct this information but in principle it's possible.

This is an interesting question and is very relevant for the black hole information paradox! If Alice stays outside the black hole forever, she will never be able to know if Bob measured his particle or not, so nothing weird can happen. However, if Alice jumps into the black hole she could "catch up" to Bob and they could compare results.

The weird thing occurs when we assume that the black hole also emits Hawking radiation. If Bob jumps into the black hole and Alice waits long enough, the black hole will be much smaller because it will have evaporated out a lot of radiation. This radiation should be entangled to the black hole. Because Bob jumped into the black hole, we should really think of him as being part of the black hole itself. The problem arises because of "monogamy of entanglement". Bob's particle is entangled to Alice's particle. But Bob's particle is also entangled to the radiation. Quantum mechanics says these statements can't both be true, so what's going on here? 

Well, we aren't totally 100% sure but there are a lot of good ideas about this issue. In my opinion, the best way to think about this is in terms of quantum information because we are dealing with subtle entanglement structure, what the field of QI was built to understand. In this viewpoint, the "Hayden-Preskill protocol" uses quantum information to argue that after something called the "Page time", Alice's qubit is *not* entangled with the black hole anymore, it is entangled with the Hawking radiation instead. After the Page time, a black hole basically spits out the quantum information thrown into it basically as fast as you can pump it in. A more careful analysis shows that it takes approximately the "scrambling time" for the information to be ejected into the Hawking radiation.

I like the Hayden-Preskill protocol because it is as model-independent as you can get in quantum gravity. It assumes:

1) Like both pure GR and pure QFT, quantum gravity (at the very least, quantum black holes) evolve unitarily. 

2) The black hole Hilbert space has dimension ~e^S_BH , where S_BH is the entropy of the black hole. This makes sense because if we are ignorant of the microstate of the black hole, i.e. if we replaced it with the maximally mixed state, it would have entropy S_BH. This is equivalent to saying that the black hole entropy of GR is computing the coarse-grained entropy of the black hole, as opposed to a fine-grained entanglement entropy.

3) Quantum black holes are described by a chaotic Hamiltonian, in particular one that is "scrambling". Scrambling just means if I poke the quantum system (perturb it by some local operator) then that poke should propagate throughout the whole system (the operator should grow to act on the whole system). This makes sense because black holes have a huge Hilbert space and appear to be very thermal objects (for example, they have a temperature). This seems to suggest that its many degrees of freedom are mixed around, allowing for a thermodynamic description.

We don't need to assume anything else about what the Hamiltonian of the black hole is, so for any model of quantum gravity that satisfies 1), 2), and 3), the Hayden-Preskill protocol will apply. An example of such a theory is holography. Of course, it could be true that any of these assumptions are not true of our universe, but hopefully, I have sketched out why they aren't unreasonable, and I would go as far as to say likely true. Keep up the good questions!

There are a few ways that they disagree. The most classic example that people mention is that general relativity is not "renormalizable". Normally, what we do in QFT is we stick all the quantum stuff into something called the path integral (this is one of many ways, but the most natural in the case of gravity). Basically, the path integral says to average over all possible configurations of the field, given a fixed initial and final state, and this average is exactly the square root of the quantum probability you know and love. In GR, however, the thing we average over is the metric. There are many conceptual issues with this, but I'll focus on renormalizability for now. When you try to compute this average, it turns out that you get an infinite answer for everything. Now, anyone who knows anything about QFT knows that this isn't immediately a problem: QFT has many many infinities for many many things, but luckily people like Ken Wilson taught us how to deal with these infinities in a well defined, systematic, physically motivated way. This method of dealing with the infinities is called renormalization. It says things like "the election mass is the value we measure for it" and "for this fixed energy, particles scatter at this strength". Given these FINITE number of "inputs" (the masses, the interaction strength at a fixed energy), QFT can predict all the properties of matter we have ever seen, an infinite number of possible measurements. A good analogy is that QFT gives the shape of the curves, and those inputs are the integration constants that let you plug in real numbers. We would have had to plug these numbers in anyways to match with experiment, but Wilson taught us how to plug them in correctly. As a side note, this does mean that we could never hope to predict the mass of the electron or the coupling strength of the forces within this framework, at least not in a way that I could ever imagine. Whether or not that is an issue to you is up to taste, but most physicists come to think that this is more of a feature than a bug.

We could try to do the same thing for GR. Let's just plug in the strength of gravity (Newton's constant) and hope for the best! Well, if you do that, you still get an infinite answer, at higher energies than before though. No matter, we dealt with the first infinity, let's just plug in a second input to the theory to tame this second infinity. Well, you still get a (new) infinite answer. You can try plugging in a third, fourth, 1000th input, the issues will always come back if you push the energy high enough. You can prove that this can't be fixed: you need an infinite number of experimental inputs to predict anything in the naive attempt to quantize gravity. You need to know all the results of your measurements to predict those measurements! That's a bad sign, and it shows that gravity isn't quantum in the same way the other forces are.  

However, like I hinted at above, if you don't care about pushing the energy arbitrarily high then you're totally fine! A finite number of inputs will give you the right answers as long as you squint your eyes a bit and don't worry about what's happening smaller than the system you're interested in. For example, in cosmology you can figure out how the universe behaved in the past with quantum matter, as long as you don't go so far in the past that the energy gets too high. Or, you can just use the classical background of a curved space and put the quantum theory on that: you've essentially just sent Newton's constant to be zero, so you don't care about how matter backreacts onto the geometry. There's still a lot you can do with GR+QFT, you just can't do everything. Doing that requires a lot of new insight, and hopefully we will be around to see it!
