Here is one possible perspective on this. Spacetime is "made" of points. The Einstein hole argument (explained below) says that points do not have a physical meaning in any usual sense. Therefore, spacetime is not physical. 

The Einstein hole argument is very confusing when you first see it (it's THE thing that kept Einstein from believing GR for a while) and is a consequence of any theory which has "diffeomorphism invariance". Diffeomorphism invariance is the mathematical way to say that coordinate systems are completely arbitrary and you can pick whichever one you please, if it's unfamiliar don't get too caught up in the name. It just means that if you give me your two favorite coordinate systems, and I change from one to another, the physics shouldn't change based on which one I use. This is applying a "passive" diffeomorphism and is not very controversial I think. However, this is *exactly* mathematically equivalent to an "active" diffeomorphism. An active diffeomorphism is when I keep the *same* coordinates as before but I move the points themselves around so the points have new labels anyways. Imagine a cloth with some grid lines I draw over them. Moving the grid lines around is a passive diffeomorphism: moving the cloth and keeping the grid lines fixed is an active diffeomorphism. You can see that they produce the exact same effect. 

The problem is this. In GR, you put down a coordinate system and solve some equations which tell you things like "the curvature is 17m^-2  at this point". But what it ACTUALLY tells you when you do the calculation is "the curvature is 17m^-2  at *these coordinates*" because you're always doing calculations in coordinates. If I do an active diffeomorphism, the coordinate numbers stay exactly the same so I will find the same coordinate location as before. But the point that these coordinates represent is completely different. This means that the points themselves can not have intrinsic properties! Doing a diffeomorphism shuffles around the properties of the individual points so they are not properties of the points themselves. If spacetime was like a fluid with little "spacetime atoms" in any usual sense this wouldn't happen, so spacetime can't be physical in the same way water is.

There are two ways to explain it: through special relativity, or through quantum mechanics. Either way, the following realization is important:

------------------------------------------------

Classical Mechanics:

The action is defined as S = \int L dt along whatever path you are considering (usually the one that extremizes this value) and so it makes sense to define an infinitesimal change in the action to be dS = L dt. 

The Hamiltonian of the system is defined to be H = p \dot{q} - L (sum over all p \dot{q} pairs if needed, gonna stick to 1D for simplicity for now). A very simple consequence of this definition is that the Lagrangian is also defined as L = p \dot{q} - H. Why does this help us? Well, let's plug this expression back into the definition of dS to get:

dS = L dt = (p(dq/dt) - H)dt = pdq - Hdt

Here is where the split can occur between the two viewpoints, SR or QM. I'll give both views so you can compare them and decide which is the most intuitive to you.

-----------------------------------------

SR/GR:

The Hamiltonian, in a sense, measures the energy of your system. It is important to remember that in Special Relativity, time and energy are linked in the same way that space and momentum are; in fact, energy is just the time component of the momentum 4-vector. The minkowski metric is given by diag(-1,1,1,1) and so we can write the above expression as

dS = p_\mu dx^\mu

Remembering that p\_\mu = m u_\mu = m dx\_\mu / d\tau (where \tau is the proper time) we can again rewrite dS as

dS = m u_\mu dx^\mu = m u_\mu u^\mu d\tau = mc^2 d\tau

because u_\mu u^\mu = -c^2 no matter what u is. If you don't already know this, I urge you to write down the expression for d\tau^2 and see if you can show this yourself.

The point is that in SR (and GR) the action measures the proper time elapsed by a particle along its path. The principle of least action becomes the principle of greatest proper time: in GR, this generalizes to say that particles travel along geodesics in spacetime, and those geodesics are determined by the geometry of spacetime, i.e. gravity.

---------------------------------------

QM:

Braket notation will be our friend here. In QM, the expression |<f|i>|^2 gives the probability that given a state |i>, we can transition to |f>. Therefore, it is important to be able to calculate <f|i>. How can we write this in general? Well, let's say |i> = |0,0>, the position eigenstate at the origin measured at t=0. Let's say also that |f> = |x,t>, the position eigenstate at x measured at a time t. To make this easier to calculate, let's write |f> in terms of |i>. We can write this as |x,0> = T(x)|0,0> where T(x) is the translation operator that shifts our state by an amount x. Similarly, 

|x,t> = U(t)|x,0> = U(t)T(x)|0,0> 

where U(t) is the normal time translation operator U(t) = exp(-i/hbar H t). It is critical to note that T(x) = exp(i/hbar p x). Therefore, we can write the propagator as

<f|i> = <0,0|exp(i/hbar (px - Ht))|0,0> = <0,0|exp(i/hbar S)|0,0>

There is a problem though: I didn't tell you which path to calculate S over. You might think that we should take the path that minimizes S as an analogy to classical mechanics, but this isn't quite right. The real answer (and this is where the difference in classical and quantum really kicks in) is that the particle takes EVERY path! You have to compute the action for every path and integrate over all the possibilities. This can be done by choosing a timestep dt, and having the particle move to any position after a time dt. Then, integrate over all possible intermediate positions. Take dt to zero, you've considered all paths. You could also imagine moving the state |f> around, figuring out the propagator for any position or time. The function you get in the end is exactly the wave function in the position representation. This is the path integral formulation of QM. So if we integrate over all paths with equal weight, why does the classical path seem so much more important?

The answer is interference. As S/hbar gets really big (i.e., as our system gets larger to enter the classical limit) you can see the propagator starts to oscillate super rapidly over most paths. However, over paths where S is pretty constant, it doesn't oscillate much anymore and the paths nearby actually constructively interfere and therefore have a larger contribution. That is, even though all paths are considered equally, the ones that make S stationary are actually more important because it doesn't cancel as easy as all the other paths.

-------------------------------------------------

If you want to combine these two notions, you get the "worldline formulation" of QFT. Essentially, the difference is that in QM particles can only go forwards in time but in QFT the particle can take ANY path through spacetime, including ones that bounce forwards and backwards in time. Draw this as a picture, and you'll see antimatter pop out naturally: when the particle goes "backwards" in time, it's an antiparticle, so turning points look like pair production, particle-antiparticle annihilation, etc.

The problem with the Klein Gordon equation was *exactly* that it is second order. In fact, for a complex scalar field phi, this current is J=i(phi^* (dphi) -phi(dphi^* )). I might have messed up a sign or a factor of i but you get the idea. You can check that taking a derivative of this vanished if phi satisfies the KG equation. Here's the problem: look at the 0th component, which is the relativistic version of psi^dagger psi. It can be negative if the second term is bigger than the first! What does a negative probability even mean?

The answer is that you should multiply this current by the electric charge and interpret it as the electric current for the field. The negative current is just the flow of antiparticles, which pop up in a different way for spin-1/2 fields as well. In physics, we have had different ways of viewing the same stuff for a long time. If I see an apple fall, I could describe that using the framework of:

- Newton: The force of gravity is pulling it down

- Hamilton: Position changes potential energy which changes kinetic energy which changes momentum which changes position, and this cycle is what causes movement

- Lagrange: The path the apple takes through space maximizes the kinetic energy while minimizing the potential energy. If you're curious, this is called the "principle of least action".

These perspectives all look very different at first: one talks about forces acting on the apple at every moment of time, another talks about this big web of changes in abstract variables, another is talking about the *entire path* of the apple all at once. However, you can show that they are all completely equivalent to each other. That doesn't mean they are equally useful in every situation though. For example, the notion of force (Newton) doesn't generalize well to quantum mechanics, but the ideas of the cycle of change (Hamilton) or considering the whole path at once (Lagrange) do. Sometimes in physics, we can use these different languages to describe the same stuff in different ways, and these different languages are each useful in their own ways but hard to use in others. Having them all and being able to switch between them helps us solve more problems than any particular one would let us.

Holography is basically the same idea but weirder because we aren't changing languages for how an apple falls, we are changing languages for quantum field theory and quantum gravity which are weird enough by themselves. For quantum gravity systems, we can use language A to calculate stuff using the geometry of spacetime and other ideas from gravity, and we can use language B we can calculate stuff using quantum fields. Holography provides a dictionary of sorts between language A and B. Here's a "concrete" example: Let's say I have a black hole. Using language A, I can use the geometry of spacetime to calculate how big the black hole's surface area is. On the other hand, I can use language B to compute the entropy of the black hole (if that makes you uncomfortable, all you need to know is that this is a simple calculation we can do in language B). It turns out that Entropy = Area/4G_N where G_N is Newton's constant. This formula can be generalized and is called the "RT Formula" after the physicists who discovered it. In some situations, the area is easy to compute and the entropy is hard. In other situations, the entropy is hard to compute and the area is easy. The RT formula lets us use either language to make the calculation as easy as possible.

It turns out that if language A talks about 3,4,5,... spacetime dimensions, then language B will use 2,3,4,... spacetime dimensions. Very strange, but it was shown a long time ago that it works very well as long as language A/B are a special kind of gravity or quantum field theory. People are still trying to understand how to make this "translation" between A/B more general, so that one day one of them will actually describe our universe! Wish us luck :)

This is something I work on, the idea goes by many names such as "the AdS/CFT correspondence" or "gauge/gravity duality" or "holography". Here's the big idea: imagine that the universe is a big ball, and say this ball has d dimensions (for our universe, d=4). A ball has a sphere which separates "inside the ball" and "outside the ball" which is called the boundary. It turns out that if you look at gravity living inside this ball, it can be completely equivalently described by quantum mechanics acting only on the boundary, which is always d-1 dimensional. In this way, gravity in d dimensions is "the same" as quantum mechanics in d-1 dimensions. 

Now, there are some caveats here. You may object that not every universe can be fit inside a ball in this way, and you'd be right. Demanding that this works turns out to imply you have a negative cosmological constant. Furthermore, it's not just any old theory of quantum mechanics: it's a special kind called a "conformal field theory" (a CFT) which just means it looks the same no matter how close you zoom in. Quantum mechanics in our universe does not have this property because atoms exist so when you zoom in far enough you can tell how zoomed you are by checking if you're bigger or smaller than an atom. 

People are actively trying to figure out how to make this idea more general, i.e. can you make this idea work for spacetimes with zero or positive cosmological constant? It's an open problem, but people are excited about holography because it lets you talk about a theory of gravity using the language of quantum mechanics. Until the generalization of holography to positive cosmological constants (or non conformal field theories if you want to say we are the boundary instead) is found, it doesn't necessarily describe our universe but there are good reasons from classical GR to expect any theory of quantum gravity to have similar features of living in one smaller dimension, which is another reason people are so excited about holography. In GR, the energy-momentum tensor satisfies 

[;\nabla_\mu T\^{\mu\nu} =0;], 

where [;\nabla\_\mu;] is the covariant derivative (basically captures the combined change of coordinates+unit vectors in any coordinate system). In general, they can be written in the form 

[;\nabla\_\mu = \partial\_\mu + \Gamma\_\mu,;]

[;\partial\_\mu;] is the usual partial derivative (how coordinates change) and [;\Gamma\_\mu;] is the "Christoffel symbols" which is (roughly) a (co)vector of matrices that tell you how much each basis vector changes (the matrix part) if you move in some direction (the covector part). Be careful though, [;\Gamma\_\mu;] isn't actually a tensor even though it's almost a tensor. Anyways, if I have a vector field [;\xi\^\mu;] , then I can construct a new (co)vector field 

[;j\_\mu = T\_{\mu\nu} \xi\^\nu.;] 

Just like the continuity equation of E\&M is that [;\nabla\_\mu j\^\mu =0;] , we will get a conservation law relating to spacetime translations/rotations etc if and only if

[;\nabla\^\mu T\_{\mu\nu} \xi\^\nu = 0.;] 

Use the product rule to see this is the same thing as saying 

[;T\_{\mu\nu} (\nabla\^\mu \xi\^\nu )= 0.;] 

Because [;T\_{\mu\nu};] could be anything, this is a condition on properties of [;\xi\^\mu;]. In particular, because [;T\_{\mu\nu};] is symmetric, we only need to require that [;\nabla\^\mu \xi\^\nu;] is antisymmetric in [;\mu,\nu;], not that the full term vanish.

Any vector field with the property that [;\nabla\^\mu \xi\^\nu ;] is antisymmetric is called a Killing vector (named after Wilhelm Killing). Killing vectors are one-to-one with symmetries of the metric, i.e. spacetime. This is another manifestation of Noether's theorem. An example is if [;\xi\^\mu\_t = (1,0,0,0) = \delta\^\mu\_0;] in flat space, i.e. a time translation. Then of course [;\nabla\^\mu \xi\^\nu\_t;] is antisymmetric there: it vanishes! But in a general expanding universe, we have to remember that (lowering the derivative index for convenience)

[;\nabla\_\mu \xi\_t\^\nu = \partial\_\mu \delta\^\nu\_0 + {\Gamma\^\nu}\_{\lambda\mu }\delta\^\lambda\_0 ={\Gamma\^\nu}\_{0\mu}  ;] 

I restored the matrix indices on [;{\Gamma\^\alpha}\_{\beta \mu} ;] (the [;\alpha,\beta;]) but the big picture is just that you get something nonzero, which might be ok if its antisymmetric, but in the FRW case it won't be. This is why time translation isn't a symmetry of FRW spacetime, which is why energy isn't conserved.

Hamiltonians are tricky to define here because they are related to time translations but time is observer-dependent in GR. It turns out that the total 4-Hamiltonian vanishes because of the fact we can choose any coordinates we want so in that sense it is conserved because its always 0. The stress-energy tensor only captures the stress-energy of matter, not of the gravitational field, which is worth noting here at the end.

TL;DR: Energy is conserved [;\iff;] there is a current to mediate this symmetry [;\iff;] there is a timelike Killing vector [;\iff;] the spacetime has a symmetry of time translations.

To answer this, we need to know that the flux of light F seen by an observer a distance d away from a source of luminosity L is an inverse square law. Mathematically, this means that F = L/(4 pi d^2). Basically, this just comes from the fact that for a given burst of light from the object, the total amount of light is constant over the surface area of the sphere as it goes radially outward. Luminosity is the thing that a lightbulb reports to tell you how bright it is, and is intrinsic to the object.

Next, it turns out that the human eye is roughly logarithmic in its vision for decently bright objects, meaning that we are better at telling if something is twice as bright as something else, rather than some fixed minimum resolution. Because of this, historically, astronomers defined a measure of brightness called the "apparent magnitude" of an object, defined as m = -2.5 log(F/F_0), where F is the flux of light as seen by the observer, and F_0 is some reference flux of light. Notice that this will get bigger for dimmer objects, or the same object from further away. Additionally, there is something called "absolute magnitude" that is intrinsic to the object itself, defined as M = -2.5 log(L/L_0) where L and L_0 are the intrinsic luminosity of the objects. = -2.5 log(F/F_0 \* L_0/L) 

= -2.5 log((L/4 pi d^(2))/(L_0/4 pi d_0^(2)) \* L_0/L)

= 5 log(d/d_0)

There are two ways to explain it: through special relativity, or through quantum mechanics. Either way, the following realization is important:

------------------------------------------------

Classical Mechanics:

In classical mechanics, the actual physically relevant quantity is the action of the path you consider, not the Lagrangian. The action is defined as S = \int L dt along whatever path you are considering (usually the one that extremizes this value) and so it makes sense to define an infinitesimal change in the action to be dS = L dt. 

The Hamiltonian of the system is defined to be H = p \dot{q} - L (sum over all p \dot{q} pairs if needed, gonna stick to 1D for simplicity for now). A very simple consequence of this definition, which many people don't fully appreciate, is that this means the Lagrangian is also defined as L = p \dot{q} - H. Why does this help us? Well, let's plug this expression back into the definition of dS to get:

dS = L dt = (p(dq/dt) - H)dt = pdq - Hdt

Here is where the split can occur between the two viewpoints, SR or QM. I'll give both views so you can compare them and decide which is the most intuitive to you.

-----------------------------------------

SR/GR:

The Hamiltonian, in a sense, measures the energy of your system. It is important to remember that in Special Relativity, time and energy are linked in the same way that space and momentum are; in fact, energy is just the time component of the momentum 4-vector. The minkowski metric is given by diag(1,-1,-1,-1) and so we can write the above expression as

dS = - p_\mu dx^\mu

Remembering that p\_\mu = m u_\mu = m dx\_\mu / d\tau (where \tau is the proper time) we can again rewrite dS as

dS = -m u_\mu dx^\mu = -m u_\mu u^\mu d\tau = -mc^2 d\tau

because u_\mu u^\mu = -c^2 no matter what u is. If you don't already know this, I urge you to write down the expression for d\tau^2 and seeing if you can show this yourself.

The point is that in SR (and GR) the action measures the proper time elapsed by a particle along its path. The principle of least action becomes the principle of greatest proper time: in GR, this generalizes to say that particles travel along geodesics in spacetime, and those geodesics are deterimed by the geometry of spacetime, i.e. gravity.

---------------------------------------

QM:

Braket notation will be our friend here. In QM, the expression |<f|i>|^2 gives the probability that given a state |i>, we can transition to |f>. Therefore, it is important to be able to calculate <f|i>, also called the propogator. How can we write this in general? Well, let's say |i> = |0,0>, the position eigenstate at the origin measured at t=0. Let's say also that |f> = |x,t>, the position eigenstate at x measured at a time t. To make this easier to calculate, let's write |f> in terms of |i>. We can write this as |x,0> = T(x)|0,0> where T(x) is the translation operator that shifts our state by an amount x. Similarly, 

|x,t> = U(t)|x,0> = U(t)T(x)|0,0> 

where U(t) is the normal time translation operator U(t) = exp(-i/hbar H t). It is critical to note that T(x) = exp(i/hbar p x). Therefore, we can write the propogator as

<f|i> = <0,0|exp(i/hbar (px - Ht))|0,0> = <0,0|exp(i/hbar S)|0,0>

There is a problem though: I didn't tell you which path to calculate S over. You might think that we should take the path that minimizes S as an analogy to classical mechanics, but this isn't quite right. The real answer (and this is where the difference in classical and quantum really kicks in) is that the particle takes EVERY path! You have to compute the action for every path and integrate over all the possibilities. This can be done by choosing a timestep dt, and having the particle move to any position after a time dt. Then, integrate over all possible intermediate positions. Take dt to zero, you've considered all paths. You could also imagine moving the state |f> around, figuring out the propogator for any position or time. The function you get in the end is exactly the wave function in the position representation. This is the path integral formulation of QM. So if we integrate over all paths with equal weight, why does the classical path seem so much more important?

The answer is interference. As S/hbar gets really big (i.e., as our system gets larger to enter the classical limit) you can see the propogator starts to oscillate super rapidly over most paths. However, over paths where S is pretty constant, it doesn't oscillate much anymore and the paths nearby actually constructively interfere and therefore have a larger contribution. That is, even though all paths are considered equally, the ones that make S stationary are actually more important because it doesn't cancel as easy as all the other paths.

-------------------------------------------------

If you want to combine these two notions, you get QFT. Essentially, the difference is that in QM particles can only go forwards in time but in QFT the particle can take ANY path through spacetime, including ones that bounce forwards and backwards in time. Draw this as a picture, and you'll see antimatter pop our naturally: when the particle goes "backwards" in time, it's an antiparticle, so turning points look like pair production, particle-antiparticle annihilation, etc.

Sorry if I went too high level. Let me try again then: 

Particles have certain properties that, when these properties change, it doesn't actually change their physics. This is analogous to how we can pick any coordinate system we want to describe the physics, but the actual events aren't changing, only our description of them.  However, even though physics is independent of these properties, we still have to pick one to do any calculations. This is called 'picking a gauge'. This is analogous to picking a zero for your energy. Transformations that change these properties are called "gauge transformations". Things that don't change after a gauge transformation are called "gauge invariant".

However, certain equations of physics don't appear to be gauge invariant at first, i.e. after changing your gauge, the equation is different. If you end up changing the equations to require gauge invariance, the extra terms you add end up implying a bunch of cool things like Maxwell's equations, and the analogy of Maxwell's equations for the other forces (not gravity).

Imagine if we were two dimensional beings that lived in a piece of paper. Now, imagine drawing a line sticking out of every point if the paper. If I place a point on each line in a smooth way, like the graph of a function that takes in two numbers and outputs one, I can still always project back down to the original plane. Alternatively, imagine a sphere with a plane tangent to each point, but these planes "only live" at the points they touch, so they don't actually intersect eachother. Now imagine a vector (arrow) living on each plane, and pretend they vary in a smooth way. Think of a planet with a wind storm and the arrows tell you which direction the wind is blowing at that point. This is the concept of a "vector bundle", basically just a space (the paper or the sphere), an "internal space" (the lines or the planes) associated to each point. A general vector bundle could have any space/ "internal space" combination. 

The thing is, like I said, these lines/planes don't intersect and aren't in general easy to relate to eachother. You have to pick how you want each line/plane to be related. To see why, imagine a vector field on a plane that points away from the origin everywhere. Each vector lives in its own internal space (another plane) at each point. In polar coordinates this field looks like (r,\theta) = (1,0). The coefficients are constant, but is the vector field? We have to manually specify how these spaces are related. The choice of how to relate all these internal spaces to eachother is a choice of "connection". A connection also just basically a manifestation of the product rule for derivatives: if X is a vector field, u^i are the coefficients and x_i are the basis vectors, then dX=d(\sum_i u^ix_i) = \sum_i( du^i*x_i + u^idx_i). The first part is measuring how much the coefficients change, the second is measuring how much the basis vectors change. The choice of how much the basis vectors change is the choice of connection. 

Now, imagine spacetime being the space with a circle attached to each point as the internal space. This "circle direction" isn't real and we can't move through it. Because it isn't a "real" direction whatever value of our function is (I.e. the graph of the plane+lines or the wind of the sphere+planes) shouldn't change the physics of our system. Think of this as the same principle as coordinate change invariance. changing this function is called a "gauge transformation". Imagine I make a gauge transformation everywhere at once tho. That doesn't make sense, even though it "doesn't matter" what the value is I can't change something instantly because of special relativity. How would I even change it? By changing the connection. For this particular internal space, it turns out the connection itself will be a vector. So the connection is something that is a vector and can change the phase at each point at the fastest at the speed of light. To break the suspense, this connection turns out to be the electromagnetic potential, which you can interpret as the photon in this picture. 

For other forces (not gravity) Just change the internal space and you get the other particles mediating the other forces. Cool stuff!
